\section*{AP \({ }^{\text {® }}\) CALCULUS BC \\ 2009 SCORING GUIDELINES (Form B)}

\section*{Question 6}

The function \(f\) is defined by the power series
\[
f(x)=1+(x+1)+(x+1)^{2}+\cdots+(x+1)^{n}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(x+1)^{n}
\]
for all real numbers \(x\) for which the series converges.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Find the interval of convergence of the power series for \(f\). Justify your answer.
\item[(b)] The power series above is the Taylor series for \(f\) about \(x=-1\). Find the sum of the series for \(f\).
\item[(c)] Let \(g\) be the function defined by \(g(x)=\int_{-1}^{x} f(t) d t\). Find the value of \(g\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\), if it exists, or explain why \(g\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\) cannot be determined.
\item[(d)] Let \(h\) be the function defined by \(h(x)=f\left(x^{2}-1\right)\). Find the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Taylor series for \(h\) about \(x=0\), and find the value of \(h\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\).
\item[(a)] The power series is geometric with ratio \((x+1)\).
The series converges if and only if \(|x+1|<1\).
Therefore, the interval of convergence is \(-2<x<0\).
OR
\[
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left|\frac{(x+1)^{n+1}}{(x+1)^{n}}\right|=|x+1|<1 \text { when }-2<x<0
\]
At \(x=-2\), the series is \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\), which diverges since the terms do not converge to 0 . At \(x=0\), the series is \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 1\), which similarly diverges. Therefore, the interval of convergence is \(-2<x<0\).
\item[(b)] Since the series is geometric,
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(x+1)^{n}=\frac{1}{1-(x+1)}=-\frac{1}{x} \text { for }-2<x<0 .
\]
\item[(c)] \(g\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\int_{-1}^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{x} d x=-\left.\ln |x|\right|_{x=-1} ^{x=-\frac{1}{2}}=\ln 2\)
\item[(d)]
\[
\begin{aligned}
& h(x)=f\left(x^{2}-1\right)=1+x^{2}+x^{4}+\cdots+x^{2 n}+\cdots \\
& h\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=f\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=\frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize}
\(3:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { identifies as geometric } \\ 1:|x+1|<1 \\ 1: \text { interval of convergence }\end{array}\right.\)
OR
\(3:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { sets up limit of ratio } \\ 1: \text { radius of convergence } \\ 1: \text { interval of convergence }\end{array}\right.\)
1 : answer
\(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \text { : antiderivative } \\ 1: \text { value }\end{array}\right.\)
\(3:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { first three terms } \\ 1: \text { general term } \\ 1: \text { value of } h\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\end{array}\right.\)
